4D.5 If a man makes a vow to God or swears an oath to bind himself by contract or binding obligation, he shall not violate his word but shall do all that he stated.
4D.9 If a young woman, who is under her father's house, makes a vow and her father hears it but says nothing then all her vows shall stand.
4D.10 A father can cancel the obligations of a vow or contract by his daughter who is in his house.
4D.11 A husband can allow or annul the vows or contracts made by his wife.
4D.12 A vow of a widow or divorced woman shall stand against her.
4D.13 If a divorced woman makes a vow while in her husband's house, her husband can affirm or annul the vow.

precepts.text: For those of you with no husband: if a woman vows in her father's house in her youth and her father disallows her, her vow does not stand, and the Lord shall forgive her because her father disallowed her. The Most High also gave the father power over the daughter.
precepts.point: If she vowed and her husband heard it and held his peace, her vow shall stand; the Most High will honor your prayer. But if her husband disallowed her on the day he heard it, he makes her vow of none effect. If your husband hears the foolishness coming out of your mouth, praying against him, and says, Lord, do not listen to that, it is of none effect. This is the power the Most High gave the husband over the wife. This is for the woman telling her husband, find yourself another wife because I am not doing what you say. Do not get mad at us; we are reading the Bible.
precepts.why:
Numbers 30:6-8 is about your prayers, sisters, and the power the Most High gave the husband over the wife. If the husband hears her vow and holds his peace, “then her vows shall stand”; but if he disallows her the day he hears it, “he shall make her vow which she vowed, and that which she uttered with her lips, wherewith she bound her soul, of none effect: and the Lord shall forgive her.” Some of you will go to the Most High praying against your husband, and he can say, Lord, do not listen to that trash.

Keep reading back in the chapter and it speaks of the father, for those of you who do not have a husband. It starts with the man: “If a man vow a vow unto the Lord, or swear an oath to bind his soul with a bond; he shall not break his word”.

Then: “If a woman also vow a vow unto the Lord, and bind herself by a bond, being in her father’s house in her youth”. Being where? In her father’s house. “And her father hear her vow, and her bond wherewith she hath bound her soul, and her father shall hold his peace at her: then all her vows shall stand”.

“But if her father disallow her in the day that he heareth; not any of her vows, or of her bonds wherewith she hath bound her soul, shall stand: and the Lord shall forgive her, because her father disallowed her.”

So God also gave the father power over the daughter. The same power the husband has over the wife’s vow, the father has over his daughter’s vow while she is in his house. That is the order the Most High set, and nobody made it up: do not get mad at us, we are reading the Bible.

precepts.text: When a man shall make a singular vow, the persons shall be for the Lord by thy estimation; the law already valued what was vowed.
precepts.point: If thou shalt forbear to vow, it shall be no sin in thee; but that which is gone out of thy lips thou shalt keep and perform. Do not suffer thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin, and do not say before the angel that it was an error.
precepts.why:
“If a man vow a vow unto the Lord, or swear an oath to bind his soul with a bond; he shall not break his word.” A vow is promising the Lord you will do a thing. The law already dealt with vows before Numbers 30: “When a man shall make a singular vow, the persons shall be for the Lord by thy estimation.”

What was vowed was valued by the priest’s estimation. The law already put a price on what a man vowed, so a vow was never a light word; it was something the Lord counted and required.

precepts.text: When thou shalt vow a vow, thou shalt not slack to pay it, for it would be sin in thee; but if thou forbear to vow, it shall be no sin in thee.
precepts.point: If thou shalt forbear to vow, it shall be no sin in thee; but that which is gone out of thy lips thou shalt keep and perform. Do not suffer thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin, and do not say before the angel that it was an error.
precepts.why:
“When thou shalt vow a vow unto the Lord thy God, thou shalt not slack to pay it: for the Lord thy God will surely require it of thee; and it would be sin in thee.” Say a man vows, Lord, if you bring this to pass I will never eat swine again; he must keep that vow. He cannot go back on it and simply ask forgiveness afterward, for the Lord will surely require it of him.

“But if thou shalt forbear to vow, it shall be no sin in thee.” There is no sin in not vowing at all. The sin is in the mouth that promises and does not perform: “That which is gone out of thy lips thou shalt keep and perform; even a freewill offering, according as thou hast vowed unto the Lord thy God, which thou hast promised with thy mouth.”

That is Numbers 30 in Moses’ own words again: he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth.

precepts.text: Pay that which thou hast vowed; better not to vow than to vow and not pay; suffer not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin, neither say before the angel that it was an error.
precepts.point: If thou shalt forbear to vow, it shall be no sin in thee; but that which is gone out of thy lips thou shalt keep and perform. Do not suffer thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin, and do not say before the angel that it was an error.
precepts.why:
Solomon carries the law of vows forward: “When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed. Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.”

“Suffer not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin; neither say thou before the angel, that it was an error: wherefore should God be angry at thy voice, and destroy the work of thine hands?” Do not let your mouth put your flesh in sin by promising what you will not do, and do not come afterward saying it was an error. A vow that is not paid makes God angry at your voice.

“For in the multitude of dreams and many words there are also divers vanities: but fear thou God.” A fool’s voice is known by multitude of words; the man who fears God does not fill his mouth with vows he cannot keep.

precepts.text: Swear not at all; let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
precepts.point: Swearing on the Bible in the court system is another matter: be subject unto the higher powers, for the powers that be are ordained of God, and you also have the option to affirm; either way, tell the truth.
precepts.why:
Christ took the law of vows further. “Again, ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time, Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths: But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God’s throne: Nor by the earth; for it is his footstool: neither by Jerusalem; for it is the city of the great King.”

“Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black. But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.” Under Christ we do not swear at all.

That is why we say the Lord’s will: the Lord’s will I will be there, the Lord’s will I will teach that day. Yea, yea and nay, nay, and nothing bound on the soul that the flesh may not perform.

precepts.text: Above all things, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath; lest ye fall into condemnation.
precepts.point: Swearing on the Bible in the court system is another matter: be subject unto the higher powers, for the powers that be are ordained of God, and you also have the option to affirm; either way, tell the truth.
precepts.why:
James says the same as Christ, and puts it first: “But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation.”

A man who vows a vow and does not perform it falls into condemnation, for the Lord will surely require it. So above all things, swear not; let your yea be yea and your nay, nay. That is why we say the Lord’s will rather than binding our souls with an oath.

precepts.text: If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature; old things are passed away, and a vow made while serving the world does not stand.
precepts.point: Swearing on the Bible in the court system is another matter: be subject unto the higher powers, for the powers that be are ordained of God, and you also have the option to affirm; either way, tell the truth.
precepts.why:
What about a vow made before you came into this truth? “Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”

A vow made while serving the world does not stand, for you were not vowing to the God of Israel then. Old things are passed away; the man who comes into Christ is a new creature, and the promises of the old man are not bound on the new.

precepts.text: All manner of sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven unto men, but the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost shall not be forgiven.
precepts.point: Swearing on the Bible in the court system is another matter: be subject unto the higher powers, for the powers that be are ordained of God, and you also have the option to affirm; either way, tell the truth.
precepts.why:
If you vowed ignorantly and could not fulfill it, there is forgiveness: “Wherefore I say unto you, All manner of sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven unto men: but the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost shall not be forgiven unto men.”

“And whosoever speaketh a word against the Son of man, it shall be forgiven him: but whosoever speaketh against the Holy Ghost, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world, neither in the world to come.” The only thing not forgiven is blasphemy against the Holy Ghost, which is speaking evil of this truth after receiving it. A vow broken in ignorance is not that.

precepts.text: Be subject unto the higher powers, for there is no power but of God; whosoever resisteth the power resisteth the ordinance of God.
precepts.point: Swearing on the Bible in the court system is another matter: be subject unto the higher powers, for the powers that be are ordained of God, and you also have the option to affirm; either way, tell the truth.
precepts.why:
Swearing on the Bible in the court system is another matter from the vows of Numbers 30. “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God. Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation.”

The court is a higher power ordained of God, so we are subject to it. You also have the option to affirm instead of swearing. Either way, tell the truth.

precepts.text: The prayer of the marriage bed: mercifully ordain that we may become aged together; that is the prayer, not a vow.
precepts.point: Marriage is not sin, but such shall have trouble in the flesh; trials will come up in a marriage that have to be fixed with the scriptures, so ask the Most High for the mercy and the strength to endure rather than vowing what you cannot uphold.
precepts.why:
On the wedding day we do not make vows in the manner of Christianity, promising things the flesh may not perform. We pray as Tobias and Sara prayed. “Then began Tobias to say, Blessed art thou, O God of our fathers, and blessed is thy holy and glorious name for ever; let the heavens bless thee, and all thy creatures.”

“Thou madest Adam, and gavest him Eve his wife for an helper and stay: of them came mankind: thou hast said, It is not good that man should be alone; let us make unto him an aid like unto himself. And now, O Lord, I take not this my sister for lust but uprightly: therefore mercifully ordain that we may become aged together. And she said with him, Amen.”

That is the prayer of the marriage bed, not a vow: that the Lord mercifully ordain that husband and wife may become aged together. We apply the scriptures to the marriage instead of binding the soul with an oath.

precepts.text: If thou marry, thou hast not sinned; nevertheless such shall have trouble in the flesh.
precepts.point: Marriage is not sin, but such shall have trouble in the flesh; trials will come up in a marriage that have to be fixed with the scriptures, so ask the Most High for the mercy and the strength to endure rather than vowing what you cannot uphold.
precepts.why:
“But and if thou marry, thou hast not sinned; and if a virgin marry, she hath not sinned. Nevertheless such shall have trouble in the flesh: but I spare you.”

Marriage is not sin, but such shall have trouble in the flesh. Trials will come up in a marriage that have to be fixed with the scriptures. That is why we do not vow on the wedding day what we cannot uphold; we ask the Most High for the mercy and the strength to endure, as Tobias prayed that they might become aged together.

precepts.text: Where no hedge is, the possession is spoiled; the covering of the house is the hedge.
precepts.point: The husband is a hedge of protection; where no hedge is, the possession is spoiled. The married woman has a covering that the widow and the divorced woman do not have.
precepts.why:
“But every vow of a widow, and of her that is divorced, wherewith they have bound their souls, shall stand against her.” She has no father or husband to disallow it, so what she vows she must perform.

“Where no hedge is, there the possession is spoiled: and he that hath no wife will wander up and down mourning.” The husband is a hedge of protection, the covering of the house. The married woman has a covering that the widow and the divorced woman do not have; where that hedge is gone, nothing stands between her and the vow she bound on her soul.

precepts.text: The husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church; therefore let the wives be to their own husbands in every thing.
precepts.point: This is the order of the house: the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church, and he is the saviour of the body; so let the wives be subject to their own husbands in every thing, even in what is vowed in prayer.
precepts.why:
If a wife vowed in her husband’s house and “her husband heard it, and held his peace at her, and disallowed her not: then all her vows shall stand.” Holding his peace is confirming it. “Every vow, and every binding oath to afflict the soul, her husband may establish it, or her husband may make it void.” But if he holds his peace day after day and then comes later to void it, “then he shall bear her iniquity”: he had the power to stop it and did not. And this runs one way; a wife cannot disallow or nullify her husband’s vow.

That is the order of the house. “Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as unto the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church: and he is the saviour of the body.”

“Therefore as the church is subject unto Christ, so let the wives be to their own husbands in every thing.” In every thing, even in what is vowed in prayer. The husband’s power over his wife’s vow is the headship of Christ over the church, set in the house.

precepts.text: If a man vow a vow unto the Lord or swear an oath, he shall not break his word; he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth. This is the law Israel was bound by when they swore concerning their daughters.
precepts.point: The question of the chapter: how shall we do for wives for them that remain, seeing we have sworn by the Lord not to give them our daughters? They made a vow, they swore to the Lord, and the law says a sworn oath must be performed; that is why they could not simply turn around and give their daughters.

note.label: Judges 21: The Oath at Mizpeh and Wives for Benjamin

precepts.why:
Here is the law Israel was bound by when they swore concerning their daughters. Moses spoke to the heads of the tribes, “This is the thing which the Lord hath commanded. If a man vow a vow unto the Lord, or swear an oath to bind his soul with a bond; he shall not break his word, he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth.”

That is why the question of the whole chapter is what it is: “How shall we do for wives for them that remain, seeing we have sworn by the Lord that we will not give them of our daughters to wives?” They made a vow, they swore to the Lord, and a sworn oath must be performed. They could not simply turn around and give their daughters; whatever proceeded out of their mouth had to stand.

precepts.text: These are the statutes between a man and his wife, and between the father and his daughter yet in her youth in her father's house.
precepts.point: This is the woman leaving her father's house for her husband's house when we live righteously; she now cares to please her husband.

note.label: Psalm 45: Thy Throne, O God, Is Forever

precepts.why:
The daughter is told to “forget also thine own people, and thy father’s house”. Numbers shows the two houses a woman belongs to: “These are the statutes, which the Lord commanded Moses, between a man and his wife, between the father and his daughter, being yet in her youth in her father’s house.”

Yet in her youth she is in her father's house, under her father; then she is a wife, under her husband. That is the move Psalm 45 speaks of: the woman leaving her father's house for her husband's house when we live righteously, so that she now cares to please her husband, and “he is thy Lord; and worship thou him.”

What you are seeing is a transference of power. When a father gives his daughter to a man, he gives up his power over his daughter to that man. If that man has that amount of power, should she not honor her husband as she honored her father? It is the same distance of respect: from children to mother, from wife to husband, from a man to Christ, from Christ to his Father. It is only the world that tells you that husband and wife are on the same level.

This is a vow a child is making to God, and the father has the power to make it of none effect.

points: And if she had at all an husband when she vowed: the husband can do the same. A married, grown woman makes a vow to the Lord, and her husband can disallow it and make it of none effect. He has the same amount of power over her as her father did.

That is why we say the Lord's will: the Lord's will I will be there, the Lord's will I will teach that day.

A vow made before you came into this truth does not stand, for you were not vowing to the God of Israel then; if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature, and old things are passed away. And if you vowed ignorantly and could not fulfill it, all manner of sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven unto men; only blasphemy against the Holy Ghost, speaking evil of this truth after receiving it, shall not be forgiven.

A daughter in her father's house in her youth who vows a vow is under her father's covering. If her father hears her vow and holds his peace, all her vows stand and every bond wherewith she hath bound her soul stands.

But if her father disallow her in the day that he heareth, not any of her vows or bonds shall stand, and the Lord shall forgive her, because her father disallowed her. That shows the power the Most High put in the man of the house: a father can hear his daughter bind herself and say no, and the Lord releases her.

The same covering passes to the husband. If a woman with a husband vows, or utters ought out of her lips wherewith she binds her soul, and her husband hears it and holds his peace in the day that he hears it, her vows stand.

But if her husband disallow her on the day that he heard it, he makes her vow of none effect, and the Lord shall forgive her. A wife could be binding herself to something she cannot perform, and her husband can step in and say, Lord, do not hear that vow, and the Most High releases her because of her husband.
Every vow of a widow, and of her that is divorced, wherewith they have bound their souls, shall stand against her. She has no father or husband to disallow it, so what she vows she must perform.
The husband is a hedge of protection; where no hedge is, the possession is spoiled. The married woman has a covering that the widow and the divorced woman do not have.

This is the order of the house: the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church, and he is the saviour of the body; so let the wives be subject to their own husbands in every thing, even in what is vowed in prayer.

If a wife vowed in her husband's house and her husband heard it and held his peace and disallowed her not, then all her vows stand. Her husband may establish every vow and every binding oath to afflict the soul, or her husband may make it void.

If he altogether holds his peace at her from day to day, then he establishes all her vows and confirms all her bonds, because he held his peace in the day that he heard them. Holding your peace is confirming it.

But if he shall any ways make them void after that he hath heard them, then he shall bear her iniquity. He cannot hear her vow, hold his peace day after day, and then come later to void it; he had the power to stop it and did not, so the iniquity falls to him. And this runs one way: a wife cannot disallow or nullify her husband's vow.

These are the statutes which the Lord commanded Moses, between a man and his wife, and between the father and his daughter, being yet in her youth in her father's house. The whole chapter is the government of vows inside the house of Israel.
